"Full-stack" means something bigger when the bottom of your stack
is a robot.

The stack in physical AI / robotics software:

→ FRONTEND: operator dashboards, fleet ops UIs (React/TypeScript)
→ BACKEND: services, APIs, orchestration (Java, Python)
→ DATA: telemetry pipelines, throughput + jam-rate streams
→ ML LAYER: forecasting, vision, optimization models
→ CONTROL: real-time commands to actuators, deterministic loops
→ HARDWARE: conveyors, robots, sensors, PLCs

A full-stack engineer here ships a feature that touches a UI a
human watches AND a motor that moves a package. That end-to-end
ownership is rare and incredibly valuable.

If you can move from a React dashboard to a Python ML service to a
control-plane reliability fix in one sprint — you're exactly the
profile physical-AI teams are hiring.

author: Abdul Ahad
text:
Two things are happening in tech right now simultaneously.

General software engineers are being laid off by the thousands.
AI engineers can't be hired fast enough.

Same industry. Same month. Opposite trajectories.

Here's the data — and which side you're actually on 👇

The numbers nobody's talking about together:
→ General software engineering jobs: down 49% from pre-pandemic baseline
→ AI and ML engineer roles: up 59% over the same period
→ Agentic AI job postings: up 10,854% year over year
→ AI skills salary premium: 43% above non-AI counterparts
→ Salesforce fiscal year 2026: zero new engineers hired

Zero.

The companies aren't shrinking.
They're replacing one type of engineer with another.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝘂𝘁:

→ Generalist developers maintaining legacy systems
→ Mid-career engineers with no AI in their stack
→ Entire support and ops engineering teams replaced by automation

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱:
→ Engineers who can build and deploy AI in production
→ Developers who design systems around LLMs not just use them
→ People who can architect agentic workflows — not just call an API

The market isn't broken.
It's bifurcated.

And the gap between both sides is getting wider every quarter.

Here's the part that should concern most developers:

Microsoft now asks candidates in interviews
how they use AI tools in their workflow
and how they'd build AI features into products.

It's not a bonus question.
It's a filter.

The degree requirement is also going.
Companies are shifting from PhD requirements to practical experience and portfolio-based hiring. Tech Jacks Solutions

Which means the credential that used to open doors
is being replaced by proof that you can ship.

I'm a Software Engineer in Lahore.

No $185K salary. No Big Tech offer. Not yet.

But I made a decision 12 months ago
to build on the right side of this split.

Schmoozzer 10X AC — agentic outreach system.
Document Intelligence AI — production NLP pipeline.
VisionsCraft — AI automation for real business workflows.

Not for a grade.
Not for a portfolio checkbox.
Because the market was already telling me which direction it was moving.

It's been telling everyone.

Most people just weren't listening.

The developers winning in 2026 aren't necessarily the smartest ones.

They're the ones who read the market early
and started building before it became obvious.

It's not too late.
But the window is closing faster than most people realize.

Are you actively upskilling toward AI or waiting to see how this plays out?

Be honest. 👇

author: Hamza Arbi
text:
I've been noticing a troubling trend in Pakistan's precision agriculture space.
Most projects and companies are hiring AI engineers and machine learning experts as their core team.


But where are the agriculture graduates? The agronomists? The plant pathologists? The soil scientists? 


The Problem:
We're building technology for agriculture — but without enough agriculture expertise in the room.
AI engineers understand models and algorithms, not why a farmer's crop is turning yellow.
Data scientists understand patterns, not how to read a field's microclimate.
ML professionals optimize for accuracy, not what a farmer actually needs to know.
The result?
Beautiful dashboards that don't solve real problems.
Impressive models that farmers never use.
Are We Building Precision Agriculture or AI Showrooms?


Technology that impresses investors but doesn't serve growers.
Why Agriculture Experts Matter:
✅ They understand the crop cycle — they know what's normal and what's not
✅ They read the field — they can diagnose problems before AI sees them
✅ They speak the farmer's language — trust and communication come naturally
✅ They know what's practical — not everything that works in a lab works in a field
✅ They bridge the gap — between technology and the soil it's meant to serve

The Right Balance:
I'm not saying we don't need AI engineers. We absolutely do.

But the team should be:
50% agriculture experts (agronomists, pathologists, soil scientists)
30% AI/data experts (engineers, developers, modelers)
20% field specialists (extension experts, farmer liaisons, implementation leads)

Technology without agriculture knowledge is just a fancy gadget.

text:
India’s GCC story is no longer about how many people we can hire.
It is about how much capability, ownership and enterprise impact we can create.

The latest shift in the GCC ecosystem is interesting:
Professionals who previously worked as data engineers, cloud engineers or AI/ML specialists are moving into roles such as applied AI, platform engineering, MLOps and AI-agent development.
This raises an important leadership question:
Are we genuinely redesigning work—or simply adding “AI” to existing job descriptions?

The next generation of GCC leadership will need to drive four transitions:
→ Workforce planning to capability architecture
→ External hiring to build, borrow and bot
→ Task execution to product and platform ownership
→ Local delivery to local decision-making and global accountability

India now has more than 2,100 GCCs, but only a small percentage have evolved into true transformation hubs with AI-led operations and enterprise-level mandates.
The GCCs that win the next decade may not necessarily be the largest.
They will be the ones that can transform existing talent, empower local leaders and convert technology capabilities into measurable business outcomes.
For GCC leaders, what requires redesign first: roles, skills, operating models or decision rights?

Why Databricks is the Backbone of Modern Data Engineering (And How to Master It)

In the early days of big data, managing pipelines felt like playing a game of technical musical chairs. You had one platform for raw storage, a completely separate cloud data warehouse for analytical SQL, and a fragile web of custom scripts holding everything together.
Fast forward to today: Databricks has shifted from "just another big data tool" to the default backbone of modern enterprise data architecture.
By pioneering the Data Lakehouse model, it bridged the gap between low-cost data lakes and high-performance warehouses, all while natively supporting ML and GenAI workflows.
Here is a complete breakdown of what you need to know about the Databricks ecosystem today 👇

1️⃣ What Data Engineers Actually Build
Medallion Architecture: Structuring data into Bronze (raw ingestion), Silver (cleaned & conformed), and Gold(business-ready aggregations) layers.
Unified Batch & Streaming: Writing pipeline logic once using Apache Spark Structured Streaming to handle low-latency streaming and scheduled batch runs seamlessly.

2️⃣ Core Features to Master
Delta Lake: Brings ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and Time Travel (data versioning) to cloud object storage.
Delta Live Tables (DLT) & Lakeflow: Declarative pipeline frameworks that automate orchestration, monitoring, and automated data quality checks.
Unity Catalog: Centralized governance for data & AI assets with fine-grained access control and end-to-end lineage tracking.
Photon Engine: A vectorized C++ engine designed to drastically accelerate query workloads while cutting cloud compute costs.
Databricks Assistant: Built-in AI copilot for writing PySpark, optimizing SQL, and debugging pipeline errors.

3️⃣ The Modern Stack & Developer Tooling
Knowing the UI isn't enough anymore. Production-grade Databricks engineering requires:
Core Skills: PySpark, Databricks SQL, and Apache Spark optimization.
IaC & CI/CD: Terraform for infrastructure provisioning, plus Databricks Asset Bundles (DABs) and Git integration for production deployments.

4️⃣ Business ROI & UK Market Demand
Eliminating Silos: Replaces expensive dual lake/warehouse setups with a single, unified Lakehouse model.
UK Career Impact: High hiring volume across London, Manchester, and major UK tech hubs.
Key Certifications: Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate & Professional.

Databricks is no longer an emerging trend , it’s a cornerstone of modern data engineering execution.

author: Diana Gokhshtein
text:
The job market is getting more specific — and that specificity is telling us something important.

I've been tracking live tech postings through AVODEAL's Job Radar for the past 30 days. 7,555 listings. And what jumped out at me wasn't what's hot — it's how precise the demand has gotten.

Security leads with 451 job title mentions (6.0%). Data Engineering sits at 400 (5.3%). AI/ML right behind at 394 (5.2%). DevOps at 376 (5.0%). Meanwhile, broad "Full Stack" postings? Still 275 listings — but no longer the dominant signal they once were.

In my experience, when hiring language gets this specific, it means companies have already burned through the generalist experiment. They know what the gap is. They're not hoping a versatile engineer will figure it out — they're writing the exact role they need.

For engineers, I'd read this as a clear signal: depth is being rewarded right now. Security, data infrastructure, and AI implementation aren't passing trends — they're showing up consistently across industries.

And for hiring teams still posting "Full Stack Developer" for a role that actually needs someone who can architect data pipelines or harden cloud environments — it might be worth asking whether your job title is attracting the person you actually need.

Specificity in the market usually runs a few months ahead of urgency.

Two markets. Two currencies. One story.

Here is what Cloud, Data and AI hiring looks like across the US and UK in July 2026.

In the UK:

Overall job postings sit 27% below pre-pandemic levels. Wage growth is at a four year low. The broader hiring market is cooling.

But AI-related postings are 127% above pre-pandemic levels.

AI job adverts in the UK rose 1,133% between 2024 and 2026 alone. 97% of UK organisations report at least one AI-related skills gap. For the first time, ManpowerGroup identified AI as the single hardest skill for UK companies to source above every other technical discipline.

Permanent salaries in UK data engineering, analytics engineering and machine learning rose 8% to 20% in 2026. Senior AI and research science leadership roles are reaching £181,000. Data Engineers at senior level are clearing £80,000 to £100,000 plus in high demand environments.
In the US:

134,000 tech workers laid off in 2026 so far. The broad market remains volatile.

But AI/ML job postings rose 163% year over year. Demand for specialist engineers has a 3.2 to 1 ratio over supply. AI/ML Engineers are commanding $170,750 at midpoint. Data Engineers sitting at $156,250. Cloud Architects at $182,000 and above at senior level.

The pattern is identical across both markets.

Generalist tech is contracting. AI and Data specialist roles are accelerating. 

The engineers caught in the middle — without clear AI or Data specialisation — are feeling the pressure. The ones with deep, verifiable expertise in Cloud, Data and AI infrastructure are in the strongest negotiating position of their careers.

What this means if you are hiring right now:

➔ Whether you are building a team in the US or the UK — the specialist talent pool is tight in both markets and moving in the same direction
➔ Salary benchmarks in both markets have moved significantly in 2026 — budgets set against 2024 data are already out of date
➔ The companies closing Cloud and Data searches fastest in both markets are the ones moving with urgency — not waiting for the broader market to soften their options
➔ Passive candidates dominate both pools — the engineers you need are not actively looking in either market

Same story. Two currencies.

Is your hiring strategy built for the market that exists - in both?

author: Yash Watwani
text:
ML Engineer vs AI Engineer: they are not the same thing

A lot of people use these titles like they’re interchangeable.

They’re not.

Here’s the simple version:

ML Engineer
- builds and deploys machine learning systems
- works with training pipelines, features, inference, evaluation, monitoring
- usually cares a lot about model performance, reliability, and productionization

AI Engineer
- builds applications around LLMs and foundation models
- works with prompts, RAG, agents, tool use, orchestration, guardrails, evaluation
- usually cares a lot about product behavior, response quality, latency, and trust

The overlap is real.  
But the focus is different.

If you are interviewing or hiring, this distinction matters because:
- one role is often more model/system heavy
- the other is often more application/workflow heavy

The biggest mistake I see is people preparing for one role and applying to the other.

author: Bradley Mileham
text:
🚀 People keep putting Quantum, AI, and Web3 into the same "next big thing" bucket.

I don't think they belong there.

🤖 AI

AI hiring is booming... but only for specialists.

ML Systems, AI Infrastructure, and GPU Engineers are in huge demand, while many general software engineering roles have become far more competitive.

The demand isn't for AI in general, it's for people with deep, specialised expertise.

⛓️ Web3

Web3 is the one people still get wrong. Over 70 crypto projects have disappeared in H1 2026 alone, funding has consolidated, and capital is flowing to a much smaller number of winners.

Yet the demand for Protocol Engineers, Distributed Systems Engineers, Cryptographers, ZK, and Security specialists remains. The market hasn't disappeared; it's become far more selective.

⚛️ Quantum

Quantum has the opposite problem: the demand is there, but the talent simply isn't.

There are only a small number of experienced researchers and engineers working in areas like QEC, quantum hardware, control systems and quantum software, meaning many companies are competing for the same people.

The bottleneck isn't funding, it's expertise.

💡 Different markets. Same lesson.

The engineers who continue to get hired aren't chasing trends. They're building deep expertise in difficult technical problems.

Whether that's Quantum, AI, or Web3, specialist knowledge continues to win.

Chase the skill, not the label.
